title: Gideon Called: The LORD Is Peace
summary: Midianite raiders swarm the land every harvest, and Israel hides in caves and cries out. God first sends a prophet to rebuke them, then the angel of the LORD calls Gideon, a frightened farmer threshing wheat in a winepress, to save Israel. Gideon asks for a sign, sees fire consume his offering, tears down his father's altar to Baal by night, and is renamed Jerubbaal. When the Midianites gather, the Spirit comes on him, but he asks God twice more for a sign with a fleece.
story: After the forty years of rest that followed Deborah, the cycle turns again, and the oppression is the most severe yet: not an occupying king but a yearly plague of raiders that leaves Israel starving. Gideon's story, which runs through chapter 8, is the longest judge narrative so far and the turning point of the book. Here the judge himself needs convincing, and the problem is not only foreign enemies but Baal worship inside the judge's own family. This chapter is the call; chapter 7 is the victory; chapter 8 is the troubling aftermath.
historical:
The Midianites were a people associated with the desert regions east and south of Canaan, in northwest Arabia and the Sinai. Moses had lived among them and married a Midianite woman (Exodus 2:15-21), but later Israel fought them (Numbers 25 and 31). Here they join with the Amalekites and the people of the east, a general term for desert tribes beyond the Jordan. Their use of camels (verse 5) was a major advantage; camels allowed raiders to cross long stretches of desert quickly and carry off plunder. When camels were first widely used this way is debated among historians, but the Gideon account is one of the Bible's earliest descriptions of camel-mounted raiding on a large scale.

The raiders came at harvest, crossed the Jordan, spread through the Jezreel Valley, and reached as far south as Gaza. Their strategy was to take or destroy the crops and livestock, leaving Israel impoverished. Gideon's clan, the Abiezrites, belonged to the tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan, and Ophrah, his hometown, has not been identified with certainty.
cultural:
Wheat was normally threshed on an open, elevated threshing floor, where the wind could carry away the chaff when the grain was tossed. A winepress was a pit or basin cut in rock for treading grapes, hidden and low. Threshing wheat in a winepress was a sign of desperation and fear: Gideon was hiding what little grain he had. The angel's greeting, mighty man of valor, is ironic at this point, though it names what Gideon will become.

Gideon's father kept an altar to Baal and an Asherah pole, a wooden cult object representing the goddess Asherah, often set beside altars. That this was a family and town shrine shows how deeply Canaanite worship had taken root in Israel. The men of the town demand Gideon's death for destroying it. Joash's answer, if Baal is a god, let him contend for himself, is a shrewd challenge: a real god wouldn't need defending. Seeing God, or even his angel, face to face was thought to bring death (compare Exodus 33:20), which is why Gideon panics in verse 22. The fleece test relied on the heavy dews that fall in the land of Israel during the dry season, which can soak wool overnight.
literary: The chapter is built around dialogue and signs. The prophet's speech (verses 7 to 10) is a brief covenant lawsuit, reminding Israel of the exodus and their disobedience, and it is left without any recorded response. The call of Gideon (11 to 24) follows a pattern seen in the call of Moses (Exodus 3 and 4): a divine encounter, a commission, an objection of weakness, a promise of God's presence (I will be with you), and a sign. Gideon's questions are honest and a little bitter: if the LORD is with us, where are his wonders? The night raid on Baal's altar (25 to 32) shows Gideon obeying, but fearfully. The chapter ends with the fleece (36 to 40), which is placed after the Spirit comes on Gideon (verse 34), a sequence that invites the reader to wonder why he still needs a sign.

outline.t: Midian ravages Israel for seven years
The angel of the LORD calls Gideon
The sign of fire and the altar called The LORD Is Peace
Gideon tears down Baal's altar and is named Jerubbaal
The Spirit comes on Gideon and he rallies the tribes

doctrines.note: Before Gideon can fight Midian, he must confront Baal in his own father's house. The chapter suggests that Israel's outward oppression was bound up with its inward unfaithfulness.
God speaks through a prophet, through the angel of the LORD, and through signs. He meets Gideon's weakness patiently, answering his requests even when they reveal a struggling faith.

The Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon (verse 34), literally clothed himself with Gideon. The Spirit equips a timid man to lead, though the fleece shows that the gift of the Spirit and the settledness of faith are not the same thing.

words.note: Gibbor, a mighty man or warrior. Paired with chayil (strength or valor), it forms the angel's greeting in verse 12. It's ironic when spoken to a man hiding in a winepress, but it expresses what God intends to make of him.

Riv, to contend, argue, or plead a case, often used of legal disputes. Joash asks whether the townsmen will contend for Baal, and Gideon is renamed Jerubbaal, meaning let Baal contend. The name becomes a standing challenge to a god who could not defend his own altar.

The name Gideon gives his altar (verse 24) combines the divine name with shalom, peace, the word for wholeness and well-being. After fearing that he would die, Gideon hears Peace be with you and names the place for it: The LORD Is Peace.
Gazzah, a fleece of wool. Gideon's tests with the fleece have given English the phrase putting out a fleece. The text records God's patient answer without holding it up as a model to imitate.

christ: Gideon's call echoes the call of Moses and shows a pattern that runs through Scripture: God choosing the weakest and least (my clan is the weakest, I am the youngest) to accomplish his purposes. Paul describes the same pattern in 1 Corinthians 1:26-29. The angel's words, Peace be with you, and Gideon's altar, The LORD Is Peace, anticipate the peace that the risen Jesus speaks to his fearful disciples (John 20:19), and Paul's statement that Christ himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). The link is thematic: in both cases the fear of meeting God is answered by his gift of peace. Hebrews 11:32 names Gideon among those who acted in faith, faith that was often weak but real.

hard.q: Was Gideon wrong to test God with the fleece, and should Christians put out fleeces today?
hard.a: Gideon's request comes after God had already promised victory and after the Spirit had come on him, which leads many interpreters to see the fleece as a sign of weak faith rather than a model. Deuteronomy 6:16 warns against putting God to the test. Gideon himself seems aware of this: he asks God not to be angry with him. Other readers stress that God graciously answered, and see the story as a picture of God's patience with the fearful. Most agree that the passage describes what Gideon did rather than prescribing a method of guidance. Christians differ on whether asking God for signs in decision-making is appropriate, but the main point of the story is that God stoops to strengthen weak faith.

questions: Gideon asked, if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? When have you asked a question like that, and what helped?
Before fighting Midian, Gideon had to tear down an idol in his own family. What idols are closest to home for you?
God answered Gideon's fleece even though he had already given his word. How do you understand God's patience with our need for reassurance?
